chunks: From him, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Musa, from al-Husayn al-Razi, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

A man came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) with two dinars and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I wish to spend them in the cause of Allah.' He said, 'Do you have parents or one of them?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Go and spend them on your parents, for that is better for you than spending them in the cause of Allah.'

So he returned and did so, and then came to him with two other dinars, saying, 'I have done so, and these are two dinars I wish to spend in the cause of Allah.' He said, 'Do you have children?' He said, 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Go and spend them on your children, for that is better for you than spending them in the cause of Allah.'

So he returned and did so, and came to him with two other dinars, saying, 'O Messenger of Allah, I have done so, and these are two other dinars I wish to spend in the cause of Allah.' He said, 'Do you have a wife?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Spend them on your wife, for that is better for you than spending them in the cause of Allah.'

So he returned and did so, and came to him with two other dinars, saying, 'O Messenger of Allah, and these are two dinars I wish to spend in the cause of Allah.' He said, 'Do you have a servant?' He said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Go and spend them on your servant, for that is better for you than spending them in the cause of Allah.'

So he did so and came to him with two other dinars, saying, 'O Messenger of Allah, and these are two dinars I wish to spend in the cause of Allah.' He said, 'Spend them, and know that they are not superior to your first two dinars.'
ai.seo_question: What is the hierarchy of spending wealth in Islam according to this hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Shia scholarly principle of *tarjih* (weighing merits), where obligatory or highly emphasized duties (like caring for parents) are ranked above voluntary acts like jihad or general charity. The Prophet’s repeated guidance establishes a hierarchical model of wealth distribution, prioritizing immediate familial dependencies before broader communal or spiritual expenditures. This hierarchy underscores that fulfilling rights of kin (*silat al-rahim*) holds greater spiritual weight than general *sabilillah* spending in this context.
